answer.rationale:
Constraints bind hard: 14 days to expiry, line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and only one decision available. Switching the primary vendor (the path memory_c2 makes attractive) is the one option that injects qualification and migration risk exactly when there is no slack to absorb a miss, so it violates the 'without increasing delivery risk' half of the objective even if the unit-cost story is real. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is the right resilience move but does not deliver the 18% spend cut this cycle, and deferring (memory_c5) is unavailable because this contract does not auto-renew and is not non-critical. That leaves the incumbent, and memory_c4 says benchmarked renegotiation has moved this incumbent on both price and payment terms, while memory_c1 says renewal preserved integration stability. So: negotiate at renewal, with market benchmarking as the lever, and treat the 18% target as the negotiation objective rather than an assumed outcome.

I want the two source records because the memories are compressed conclusions, not evidence. memory_c2 is the strongest pull toward switching and I need to know whether the sharp cost cut and quick onboarding applied to a component of comparable criticality and lead time, or to something peripheral where a stumble was survivable; if the former, a switch becomes a real candidate for the next cycle. memory_c4 matters because the whole plan rests on the magnitude of concession it actually produced -- 'real margin' could be 4% or 20%, and if it was low single digits then negotiation alone cannot meet the mandate and I should be assembling a combined package or escalating the shortfall to finance now rather than discovering it in 14 days.

Two risks I am carrying forward rather than resolving. First, memory_c6 offers multi-year volume pricing, which is the easiest way to book a headline cost reduction -- but locking multiple years to hit a one-year target trades away the option to add the second source or switch later, and it converts a single-source exposure into a contractual one. I will not accept a multi-year term this cycle absent explicit volume-flex and exit provisions. Second, an 18% spend cut extracted from an incumbent tends to reappear as quietly narrowed service scope, thinner expedite support, or lengthened lead times -- degradation that shows up in later cycles and is easy to misattribute. memory_c6 claims the longer term did not narrow scope, which is reassuring but is exactly the kind of claim worth checking against the contract rather than the memory. So I will require scope, lead time, and expedite terms to be written unchanged, and record explicitly that this cycle's savings came with the second source still outstanding, so the next reviewer inherits the gap and not just the win. These memories are generally reliable and I am reasoning from them, but they record what worked once under conditions I cannot fully see, and none of them was formed with the line at 94% and no buffer.
